content: Cervical cancer screening has traditionally relied on cervical cytology. However, due to the established causal relationship between human papillomavirus (HPV) infection and the development of cervical cancer, HPV testing has been proposed as an alternative screening method. The objective of this study was to evaluate the diagnostic accuracy of HPV testing in detecting histologically confirmed cervical intraepithelial neoplasias (CIN) of grade 2 or worse (CIN 2+), including adenocarcinoma in situ, in women undergoing primary cervical cancer screening. Additionally, the study aimed to compare the accuracy of HPV testing to that of cytological testing, including both liquid-based cytology (LBC) and conventional cytology (CC), at various diagnostic thresholds. A systematic review of the literature was conducted, including studies published between 1992 and November 2015 in MEDLINE and Embase. The reference lists of retrieved articles were also manually searched. Studies were included if they compared the accuracy of HPV testing and cytology, with all participants undergoing both tests followed by disease verification using a reference standard. Only studies involving women participating in routine cervical cancer screening, without prior cytological abnormalities, were included. Data from the studies were extracted into 2x2 tables, detailing the number of true positives (TP), false positives (FP), true negatives (TN), and false negatives (FN) for each test. Sensitivity (TP/(TP + FN)) and specificity (TN/(TN + FP)) were calculated for each test, and relative sensitivity and specificity were determined by comparing one test to another. The Quality Assessment of Diagnostic Accuracy Studies (QUADAS) tool was used to assess potential bias in the included studies. A bivariate random-effects model was employed to compute pooled accuracy estimates, accounting for variability within and between studies as well as the intrinsic correlation between sensitivity and specificity. A total of 40 studies, involving over 140,000 women aged 20 to 70 years, were included in the review. Most studies were at low risk of bias and employed robust methodologies. Comparisons were made between hybrid capture 2 (HC2) testing (at a threshold of 1 pg/mL) and conventional cytology (CC) or liquid-based cytology (LBC) at thresholds of atypical squamous cells of undetermined significance (ASCUS+) and low-grade squamous intraepithelial lesions (LSIL+). Other high-risk HPV tests were also compared to CC and LBC at the same thresholds. For detecting CIN 2+, the pooled sensitivity estimates were 89.9% for HC2, 62.5% for CC, and 72.9% for LBC (ASCUS+ threshold). The pooled specificity estimates were 89.9% for HC2, 96.6% for CC, and 90.3% for LBC. These results were consistent across age groups (younger or older than 30 years) and in studies without verification bias. However, the accuracy of HC2 was higher in European countries compared to other regions. Sensitivity estimates for LBC ranged from 52% to 94%, while those for HC2 ranged from 61% to 100%. The quality of evidence for sensitivity was moderate, while the evidence for specificity was high. The relative sensitivity of HC2 compared to CC for detecting CIN 2+ was 1.52 (95% CI: 1.24 to 1.86), and the relative specificity was 0.94 (95% CI: 0.92 to 0.96). When comparing HC2 to LBC for CIN 2+, the relative sensitivity was 1.18 (95% CI: 1.10 to 1.26), and the relative specificity was 0.96 (95% CI: 0.95 to 0.97). For detecting CIN 3+, the relative sensitivity of HC2 compared to CC was 1.46 (95% CI: 1.12 to 1.91), with a relative specificity of 0.95 (95% CI: 0.93 to 0.97). When comparing HC2 to LBC for CIN 3+, the relative sensitivity was 1.17 (95% CI: 1.07 to 1.28), and the relative specificity was 0.96 (95% CI: 0.95 to 0.97). In conclusion, HPV testing is more sensitive than cytology for detecting CIN 2+ and CIN 3+, meaning it is less likely to miss cases of significant cervical abnormalities. However, HPV testing results in a higher number of false positives, leading to more unnecessary referrals. A negative HPV test is more reassuring than a negative cytological test, as cytology has a higher likelihood of false negatives, which could delay appropriate treatment. Further evidence from prospective longitudinal studies is needed to fully understand the clinical implications of these screening methods.
